activities.anchor: is a comparison frozen into a number
activities.caption: pair each form of comparison with its meaning
activities.name: rppFormMatch

config.prompt: Pair each form of comparison with what it is:

pairs.right: a comparison frozen into a number — 3:2 flour to water
a ratio out of 100 — a common yardstick
the assumption that a ratio stays fixed as quantities change

config.why: Nearly every headline statistic, shop discount, recipe, map scale and exchange rate is one of these three.

activities.caption: rational or irrational — file each number
activities.name: rppZooSort

config.prompt: File each number under its species:
config.why: Irrationals are more numerous in a precise sense (Cantor, 1874): throw a dart at the number line and it hits an irrational with probability 1 — the fractions, infinite as they are, are a dust.

activities.anchor: do all the algebra: multiplying powers
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the three index laws
activities.name: rppIndexCloze

config.text: The three index laws: multiplying powers %%0%% indices (2³ × 2² = 2⁵), dividing %%1%% them (2⁵ ÷ 2² = 2³), and a power of a power %%2%% them ((2²)³ = 2⁶) — each law is just counting the multiplications.
config.hint: Count the multiplications each move performs.

activities.anchor: a negative index makes a negative number
activities.caption: find the index error
activities.name: rppNegSpot

config.prompt: One of these index claims is wrong — click it:
lines: a⁰ = 1, so that dividing a³ by a³ gives a⁰ = 1.
config.correction: 2⁻³ = 1/8, a small positive number — the minus sign sends you below 1, never below 0.
config.why: A negative index makes a reciprocal, not a negative.

activities.caption: call the virus count across a cell
activities.name: rppVirusEst

config.prompt: A virus is 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ m long; a red blood cell is 7.5 × 10⁻⁶ m. Roughly how many viruses would span the cell?
config.why: (7.5 ÷ 1.2) × 10⁻⁶⁻⁽⁻⁷⁾ = 6.25 × 10¹ = 62.5 — without the notation, that comparison is an error factory.
config.context: standard form multiplies the As and adds the indices

activities.caption: direct versus inverse — drag the divider
activities.name: rppPropCompare

config.prompt: Two kinds of proportion — drag the divider:

before.label: direct
before.text: double the flour, double the water — the ratio stays fixed (y ∝ x)

after.label: inverse
after.text: more workers, fewer days — the product stays fixed (6 builders × 12 days = 9 builders × 8 days)

config.why: The honest test is always: what quantity is actually constant? Mixing the two up is the classic trap.

config.prompt: Prize money of £600 is split 2 : 3 : 5. Roughly how much does the middle share get?
config.why: 10 parts, so one part is £60 — £120, £180 and £300, whose sum checks back to £600.
config.context: the unitary method: find one part, scale to any total

activities.caption: bet before you read on — the up-then-down trap
activities.name: rppSuccPredict

config.q: A price rises 10%, then falls 10%. Where does it end?
choices: Exactly where it started — the changes cancel
1% down — the second 10% is taken of a bigger base
config.why: ×1.1 × 0.9 = ×0.99 — a net 1% loss. Percentages compound, they do not add.

activities.anchor: money at r% interest doubles in roughly
activities.caption: drop the marker — the doubling time
activities.name: rppRulePlace

config.prompt: Money at 7.2% a year doubles in roughly how many years (rule of 72)?
config.why: 72 ÷ 7.2 = 10 years — the rule of 72 turns any growth rate into a doubling time in one division.

activities.anchor: The lily-pond that fills on day 30
activities.caption: the pond on day 29
activities.name: rppLilyBranch

config.root: A lily pond fills completely on day 30. On day 29, how full is it?

choices.label: Mostly full — it grew steadily
choices.feedback: It was half empty: exponential growth is constant-ratio, starting slow — thirty doublings later the number is a billion.

choices.label: Half empty
choices.feedback: Right — the scary part of 'exponential' is not speed but constant ratio: the doubling from 1 to 2 looks trivial.

choices.label: Empty — all the growth happens on the last day
choices.feedback: The growth happened every day, equally in ratio — each day doubled the coverage.

slow.text: Constant ratio means each day doubles, so the second half of the pond fills in the final day alone.

last.text: Every day did the same multiplicative work — that is why the end looks sudden.

config.why: Equal ratios in equal times: the graph curves upward ever more steeply, and the lily-pond that fills on day 30 was half empty on day 29.
